Anthropic and Google released new frontier AI models this week, 24 hours apart. On the independent Artificial Analysis index, @AnthropicAI's Claude Fable 5.2 leads at 65, @GoogleDeepMind's Gemini 4 Carbon is on 60, and @OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra, first in September, is third at 57.

Lab-run scores unless independently tested.

Claude Fable 5.2 (9 November)

@AnthropicAI calls it a model for "the most daunting technical challenges". Twin model Claude Mythos 5.2 has fewer cybersecurity and biology safeguards, and is available only to vetted organisations (Anthropic).

• 1M token context, 128K output
• $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output, 20% cheaper than Fable 5.1 and up to 30% faster, Anthropic says
• $26.54 per task at max effort, vs $7.76 for Carbon on high (Artificial Analysis)
• One engineer had it coordinate more than 1,000 subagents for eight days; they built a prototype OS that boots on a laptop
• 1,000 Fable agents formalised the proof of Fermat's Last Theorem in 30 hours, vs 11 days for an earlier research version
• Solved two open problems in black hole physics and designed three working electronic devices from a one-paragraph prompt (Anthropic)

Gemini 4 Carbon (public 10 November)

Announced 28 October for cybersecurity defenders. Google says Gemini 4 Argon is still the pick for most work, and Carbon is for the hardest problems.

• $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output until 30 November, then $4 and $20 (Google)
• Around a fifth of Astra's price and a quarter of Fable 5.2's; cheaper per token is not always cheaper per task (The Verge)
• Gemini app: Google AI Ultra subscribers only
• Google says it leads CursorBench 4.0, Perplexity's WANDR and Zapier's AutomationBench
• 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro, 54.8% on ExploitGym, 71.0% on CWE-bench; every prompt injection blocked in Gray Swan's benchmark, Google says
• A "swarm" feature turns one prompt into a team of agents in Google's Antigravity (The Verge)

GPT-6 Astra (3 September)

@OpenAI's newest release is GPT-6.1 Terra (26 October). Astra remains its most capable model.

• $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output. 1.05M token context, 128K output (OpenAI)
• 98% on FrontierMath Tier 4; OpenAI says it helped prove a new bound on gaps between prime numbers, from 240 to 186
• 99.9% on ARC-AGI-3 on OpenAI's API harness; 62.7% on the ARC Prize's standard harness, more than double the previous best (The Batch)

Head to head (Artificial Analysis unless noted)

• FrontierSWE v2 (Anthropic): Fable 69.9%, Astra 65.5%, Carbon 61.2%
• Terminal-Bench 4.0: Carbon 65.2%, Fable 59.6%; Carbon also tops Cursor's benchmark (Cursor)
• AutomationBench (Anthropic): Carbon 53.9%, Fable 51.4%, Astra 41.4%
• OSWorld 2.1 (Anthropic): Fable 89.3%, Carbon 81.5%, Astra 79.5%
• Access: Astra is in ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business and Enterprise

Fable is the strongest, Carbon is the best value, Astra is the most widely available.

Anthropic is offering 825 million shares at $70 to $78 and plans to list on Nasdaq as "ANT" (Anthropic). Reuters puts the raise at up to $64.4 billion and the valuation at up to $1.4 trillion. First-half 2026 revenue was $16.29 billion, up from $1.16 billion a year earlier, with more than $600 billion committed to computing over the next decade (Reuters).

Cyber tools are being gated: Anthropic's Mythos, Google's Fairwind Program and OpenAI's GPT-6 Cyber (5 November). Anthropic's testers say Fable 5.2 admits when it does not know something.

It’s not easy being one of Silicon Valley’s favorite benchmarks. 

SWE-Bench (pronounced “swee bench”) launched in November 2024 to evaluate an AI model’s coding skill, using more than 2,000 real-world programming problems pulled from the public GitHub repositories of 12 different Python-based projects. 

In the months since then, it’s quickly become one of the most popular tests in AI. A SWE-Bench score has become a mainstay of major model releases from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google—and outside of foundation models, the fine-tuners at AI firms are in constant competition to see who can rise above the pack. The top of the leaderboard is a pileup between three different fine tunings of Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet model and Amazon’s Q developer agent. Auto Code Rover—one of the Claude modifications—nabbed the number two spot in November, and was acquired just three months later.

Despite all the fervor, this isn’t exactly a truthful assessment of which model is “better.” As the benchmark has gained prominence, “you start to see that people really want that top spot,” says John Yang, a researcher on the team that developed SWE-Bench at Princeton University. As a result, entrants have begun to game the system—which is pushing many others to wonder whether there’s a better way to actually measure AI achievement.

Developers of these coding agents aren’t necessarily doing anything as straightforward cheating, but they’re crafting approaches that are too neatly tailored to the specifics of the benchmark. The initial SWE-Bench test set was limited to programs written in Python, which meant developers could gain an advantage by training their models exclusively on Python code. Soon, Yang noticed that high-scoring models would fail completely when tested on different programming languages—revealing an approach to the test that he describes as “gilded.”

“It looks nice and shiny at first glance, but then you try to run it on a different language and the whole thing just kind of falls apart,” Yang says. “At that point, you’re not designing a software engineering agent. You’re designing to make a SWE-Bench agent, which is much less interesting.”

The SWE-Bench issue is a symptom of a more sweeping—and complicated—problem in AI evaluation, and one that’s increasingly sparking heated debate: The benchmarks the industry uses to guide development are drifting further and further away from evaluating actual capabilities, calling their basic value into question. Making the situation worse, several benchmarks, most notably FrontierMath and Chatbot Arena, have recently come under heat for an alleged lack of transparency. Nevertheless, benchmarks still play a central role in model development, even if few experts are willing to take their results at face value. OpenAI cofounder Andrej Karpathy recently described the situation as “an evaluation crisis”: the industry has fewer trusted methods for measuring capabilities and no clear path to better ones. 

“Historically, benchmarks were the way we evaluated AI systems,” says Vanessa Parli, director of research at Stanford University’s Institute for Human-Centered AI. “Is that the way we want to evaluate systems going forward? And if it’s not, what is the way?”

A growing group of academics and AI researchers are making the case that the answer is to go smaller, trading sweeping ambition for an approach inspired by the social sciences. Specifically, they want to focus more on testing validity, which for quantitative social scientists refers to how well a given questionnaire measures what it’s claiming to measure—and, more fundamentally, whether what it is measuring has a coherent definition. That could cause trouble for benchmarks assessing hazily defined concepts like “reasoning” or “scientific knowledge”—and for developers aiming to reach the much–hyped goal of artificial general intelligence—but it would put the industry on firmer ground as it looks to prove the worth of individual models.

“Taking validity seriously means asking folks in academia, industry, or wherever to show that their system does what they say it does,” says Abigail Jacobs, a University of Michigan professor who is a central figure in the new push for validity. “I think it points to a weakness in the AI world if they want to back off from showing that they can support their claim.”

The limits of traditional testing

If AI companies have been slow to respond to the growing failure of benchmarks, it’s partially because the test-scoring approach has been so effective for so long. 

One of the biggest early successes of contemporary AI was the ImageNet challenge, a kind of antecedent to contemporary benchmarks. Released in 2010 as an open challenge to researchers, the database held more than 3 million images for AI systems to categorize into 1,000 different classes.

Crucially, the test was completely agnostic to methods, and any successful algorithm quickly gained credibility regardless of how it worked. When an algorithm called AlexNet broke through in 2012, with a then unconventional form of GPU training, it became one of the foundational results of modern AI. Few would have guessed in advance that AlexNet’s convolutional neural nets would be the secret to unlocking image recognition—but after it scored well, no one dared dispute it. (One of AlexNet’s developers, Ilya Sutskever, would go on to cofound OpenAI.)

A large part of what made this challenge so effective was that there was little practical difference between ImageNet’s object classification challenge and the actual process of asking a computer to recognize an image. Even if there were disputes about methods, no one doubted that the highest-scoring model would have an advantage when deployed in an actual image recognition system.

But in the 12 years since, AI researchers have applied that same method-agnostic approach to increasingly general tasks. SWE-Bench is commonly used as a proxy for broader coding ability, while other exam-style benchmarks often stand in for reasoning ability. That broad scope makes it difficult to be rigorous about what a specific benchmark measures—which, in turn, makes it hard to use the findings responsibly. 

Where things break down

Anka Reuel, a PhD student who has been focusing on the benchmark problem as part of her research at Stanford, has become convinced the evaluation problem is the result of this push toward generality. “We’ve moved from task-specific models to general-purpose models,” Reuel says. “It’s not about a single task anymore but a whole bunch of tasks, so evaluation becomes harder.”

Like the University of Michigan’s Jacobs, Reuel thinks “the main issue with benchmarks is validity, even more than the practical implementation,” noting: “That’s where a lot of things break down.” For a task as complicated as coding, for instance, it’s nearly impossible to incorporate every possible scenario into your problem set. As a result, it’s hard to gauge whether a model is scoring better because it’s more skilled at coding or because it has more effectively manipulated the problem set. And with so much pressure on developers to achieve record scores, shortcuts are hard to resist.

For developers, the hope is that success on lots of specific benchmarks will add up to a generally capable model. But the techniques of agentic AI mean a single AI system can encompass a complex array of different models, making it hard to evaluate whether improvement on a specific task will lead to generalization. “There’s just many more knobs you can turn,” says Sayash Kapoor, a computer scientist at Princeton and a prominent critic of sloppy practices in the AI industry. “When it comes to agents, they have sort of given up on the best practices for evaluation.”

In a paper from last July, Kapoor called out specific issues in how AI models were approaching the WebArena benchmark, designed by Carnegie Mellon University researchers in 2024 as a test of an AI agent’s ability to traverse the web. The benchmark consists of more than 800 tasks to be performed on a set of cloned websites mimicking Reddit, Wikipedia, and others. Kapoor and his team identified an apparent hack in the winning model, called STeP. STeP included specific instructions about how Reddit structures URLs, allowing STeP models to jump directly to a given user’s profile page (a frequent element of WebArena tasks).

This shortcut wasn’t exactly cheating, but Kapoor sees it as “a serious misrepresentation of how well the agent would work had it seen the tasks in WebArena for the first time.” Because the technique was successful, though, a similar policy has since been adopted by OpenAI’s web agent Operator. (“Our evaluation setting is designed to assess how well an agent can solve tasks given some instruction about website structures and task execution,” an OpenAI representative said when reached for comment. “This approach is consistent with how others have used and reported results with WebArena.” STeP did not respond to a request for comment.)

Further highlighting the problem with AI benchmarks, late last month Kapoor and a team of researchers wrote a paper that revealed significant problems in Chatbot Arena, the popular crowdsourced evaluation system. According to the paper, the leaderboard was being manipulated; many top foundation models were conducting undisclosed private testing and releasing their scores selectively.

Today, even ImageNet itself, the mother of all benchmarks, has started to fall victim to validity problems. A 2023 study from researchers at the University of Washington and Google Research found that when ImageNet-winning algorithms were pitted against six real-world data sets, the architecture improvement “resulted in little to no progress,” suggesting that the external validity of the test had reached its limit.

Going smaller

For those who believe the main problem is validity, the best fix is reconnecting benchmarks to specific tasks. As Reuel puts it, AI developers “have to resort to these high-level benchmarks that are almost meaningless for downstream consumers, because the benchmark developers can’t anticipate the downstream task anymore.” So what if there was a way to help the downstream consumers identify this gap?

In November 2024, Reuel launched a public ranking project called BetterBench, which rates benchmarks on dozens of different criteria, such as whether the code has been publicly documented. But validity is a central theme, with particular criteria challenging designers to spell out what capability their benchmark is testing and how it relates to the tasks that make up the benchmark.

“You need to have a structural breakdown of the capabilities,” Reuel says. “What are the actual skills you care about, and how do you operationalize them into something we can measure?”

The results are surprising. One of the highest-scoring benchmarks is also the oldest: the Arcade Learning Environment (ALE), established in 2013 as a way to test models’ ability to learn how to play a library of Atari 2600 games. One of the lowest-scoring is the Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) benchmark, a widely used test for general language skills; by the standards of BetterBench, the connection between the questions and the underlying skill was too poorly defined.

BetterBench hasn’t meant much for the reputations of specific benchmarks, at least not yet; MMLU is still widely used, and ALE is still marginal. But the project has succeeded in pushing validity into the broader conversation about how to fix benchmarks. In April, Reuel quietly joined a new research group hosted by Hugging Face, the University of Edinburgh, and EleutherAI, where she’ll develop her ideas on validity and AI model evaluation with other figures in the field. (An official announcement is expected later this month.) 

Irene Solaiman, Hugging Face’s head of global policy, says the group will focus on building valid benchmarks that go beyond measuring straightforward capabilities. “There’s just so much hunger for a good benchmark off the shelf that already works,” Solaiman says. “A lot of evaluations are trying to do too much.”

Increasingly, the rest of the industry seems to agree. In a paper in March, researchers from Google, Microsoft, Anthropic, and others laid out a new framework for improving evaluations—with validity as the first step. 

“AI evaluation science must,” the researchers argue, “move beyond coarse grained claims of ‘general intelligence’ towards more task-specific and real-world relevant measures of progress.” 

Measuring the “squishy” things

To help make this shift, some researchers are looking to the tools of social science. A February position paper argued that “evaluating GenAI systems is a social science measurement challenge,” specifically unpacking how the validity systems used in social measurements can be applied to AI benchmarking. 

The authors, largely employed by Microsoft’s research branch but joined by academics from Stanford and the University of Michigan, point to the standards that social scientists use to measure contested concepts like ideology, democracy, and media bias. Applied to AI benchmarks, those same procedures could offer a way to measure concepts like “reasoning” and “math proficiency” without slipping into hazy generalizations.

In the social science literature, it’s particularly important that metrics begin with a rigorous definition of the concept measured by the test. For instance, if the test is to measure how democratic a society is, it first needs to establish a definition for a “democratic society” and then establish questions that are relevant to that definition. 

To apply this to a benchmark like SWE-Bench, designers would need to set aside the classic machine learning approach, which is to collect programming problems from GitHub and create a scheme to validate answers as true or false. Instead, they’d first need to define what the benchmark aims to measure (“ability to resolve flagged issues in software,” for instance), break that into subskills (different types of problems or types of program that the AI model can successfully process), and then finally assemble questions that accurately cover the different subskills.

It’s a profound change from how AI researchers typically approach benchmarking—but for researchers like Jacobs, a coauthor on the February paper, that’s the whole point. “There’s a mismatch between what’s happening in the tech industry and these tools from social science,” she says. “We have decades and decades of thinking about how we want to measure these squishy things about humans.”

Even though the idea has made a real impact in the research world, it’s been slow to influence the way AI companies are actually using benchmarks. 

The last two months have seen new model releases from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta, and all of them lean heavily on multiple-choice knowledge benchmarks like MMLU—the exact approach that validity researchers are trying to move past. After all, model releases are, for the most part, still about showing increases in general intelligence, and broad benchmarks continue to be used to back up those claims. 

For some observers, that’s good enough. Benchmarks, Wharton professor Ethan Mollick says, are “bad measures of things, but also they’re what we’ve got.” He adds: “At the same time, the models are getting better. A lot of sins are forgiven by fast progress.”

For now, the industry’s long-standing focus on artificial general intelligence seems to be crowding out a more focused validity-based approach. As long as AI models can keep growing in general intelligence, then specific applications don’t seem as compelling—even if that leaves practitioners relying on tools they no longer fully trust. 

“This is the tightrope we’re walking,” says Hugging Face’s Solaiman. “It’s too easy to throw the system out, but evaluations are really helpful in understanding our models, even with these limitations.”

Russell Brandom is a freelance writer covering artificial intelligence. He lives in Brooklyn with his wife and two cats.

AI term of the day: Benchmark

A benchmark is a standard test used to compare AI models. Every time a new model launches, you'll see charts showing it scored higher than the others on tests with names like MMLU, GSM8K or SWE-bench.

Each benchmark checks a different skill. MMLU asks thousands of multiple-choice questions across subjects like law, medicine and history. GSM8K tests school-level maths word problems. SWE-bench checks whether a model can fix real bugs in real software projects. Because everyone uses the same questions, the scores give a rough way to compare models side by side.

So treat benchmarks like a CV. They help you decide who to shortlist, but they don't tell you who will do the job well. The real test is to take 20 or 30 questions from your own work, run them through the models you're considering, and see which one actually gets them right.

Running LLM inference on a unified GPU cluster is an architectural waste.

LLM serving has two fundamentally different compute phases: Prefill and Decode. 

Prefill processes the input prompt in parallel. It is compute-bound, demanding massive raw TFLOPS to process thousands of tokens at once.

Decode generates output tokens one by one. It is memory-bandwidth bound, spending most of its time fetching weights from HBM to compute a single token. 

When you run both on the same GPU, your compute engine sits idle during Decode, and your memory pipeline chokes during Prefill. 

The industry is moving to Prefill/Decode Disaggregation. By splitting the serving infrastructure into specialized clusters—high-compute nodes for Prefill and high-bandwidth nodes for Decode connected via ultra-fast optical interconnects—we maximize hardware efficiency and slash latency.

Stop running heterogeneous workloads on homogeneous hardware.

Here is a profile overview of 10 key technical and executive leaders driving engineering, research, and technology platforms at NVIDIA:

1. Ian Buck – Vice President, Accelerated Computing

Ian Buck is widely recognized as the father of CUDA, the software architecture that unlocked the power of GPUs for general-purpose parallel computing and catalyzed modern AI. After developing CUDA during his Ph.D. at Stanford, he joined NVIDIA in 2004 and currently oversees the company’s enterprise and hyperscale data center AI business units. His leadership spans hardware architecture and software ecosystems, making him a pivotal architect of NVIDIA's full-stack data center strategy.

2. Gilad Shainer – Senior Vice President, Networking & Marketing

Gilad Shainer joined NVIDIA following the acquisition of Mellanox Technologies, where he played a central role in shaping high-performance InfiniBand and Ethernet interconnects. He leads NVIDIA’s networking initiatives, focusing on data-center-scale architectures and interconnect platforms like NVLink and Quantum InfiniBand. His team ensures that clusters of tens of thousands of GPUs can communicate seamlessly to train massive generative AI models.

3. Bryan Catanzaro – Vice President, Applied Deep Learning Research

Bryan Catanzaro leads NVIDIA’s Applied Deep Learning Research division, which bridges foundational AI research and real-world application across products. He pioneered early deep learning frameworks (including DeepSpeech during a stint at Baidu) and has contributed heavily to foundational AI models, DLSS (Deep Learning Super Sampling), and speech synthesis. Under his guidance, his team focuses on expanding the capabilities of open foundation LLMs and AI for graphics processing.

4. Bill Dally – Chief Scientist & Senior Vice President of Research

Bill Dally is NVIDIA’s Chief Scientist and head of NVIDIA Research, having joined the company in 2009 after serving as Chairman of Stanford’s Computer Science department. A legendary computer architect with over 120 patents, Dally’s research teams pioneer advancements in low-precision AI training, specialized chiplet architectures, and optical interconnect technology. He was honored with the prestigious 2025 Queen Elizabeth Prize for Engineering for his contributions to computing.

5. Michael Kagan – Chief Technology Officer (CTO)

Michael Kagan became NVIDIA’s CTO in May 2020 after the Mellanox acquisition, where he had served as co-founder and CTO since 1999. Previously an architecture leader at Intel, Kagan leads the technical vision for NVIDIA’s data center infrastructures, known as "AI Factories." His work focuses on integrating computing, storage, and networking hardware into unified data-center-scale processing systems.

6. Jan Kautz – Vice President, Learning & Perception Research

Jan Kautz leads NVIDIA’s computer vision, visual perception, and machine learning research groups. Before joining NVIDIA, he spent years in academia investigating computer graphics and rendering systems. Today, his team drives fundamental advances in multi-modal LLMs, 2D/3D visual understanding, efficient neural network pruning, and embodied AI foundations like the GR00T humanoid robotics platform.

7. Rev Lebaredian – Vice President, Omniverse & Simulation Technology (see 3rd image below)

Rev Lebaredian oversees the development of NVIDIA Omniverse, the company’s platform for real-time 3D simulation, digital twins, and industrial metaverses. With over 30 years in graphics engineering—including work for major Hollywood studios—Lebaredian has been a central architect of physics simulation software. His work enables researchers to train autonomous robots and physical AI inside physically accurate, synthetic virtual worlds before deploying them in reality.

8. Deepu Talla – Vice President & General Manager, Robotics & Edge AI

Deepu Talla leads NVIDIA’s Autonomous Machines business unit, focusing on edge computing, industrial automation, and robotics. Holding a Ph.D. in Computer Engineering from UT Austin, he oversees platforms like NVIDIA Jetson and Isaac. His team drives the deployment of AI-powered vision, autonomous mobile robots (AMRs), and smart-factory solutions across global manufacturing supply chains.

9. Kimberly Powell – Vice President, Healthcare

Kimberly Powell joined NVIDIA in 2008 and oversees the company's global healthcare and life sciences business. With a background in electrical and computer engineering, she led the rollout of Clara Holoscan (for medical device processing) and BioNeMo (for generative AI in drug discovery). Her organization focuses on applying GPU acceleration to diagnostic imaging, genomics, and clinical workflow analytics.

10. Mike Houston – Vice President & Chief Architect, AI Systems

Mike Houston is a principal architect behind NVIDIA’s supercomputing infrastructures, including DGX SuperPODs and large-scale GPU cluster designs. Having earned his Ph.D. from Stanford focusing on streaming architectures, Houston bridges system software, hardware design, and cluster management. His architecture teams focus on scaling GPU communication topologies to maximize throughput for trillion-parameter AI models.

So the k-means step that Faiss's docs warn "is going to be slow" for big IVF indexes now has a much faster option

An IVF index splits your vectors into lists and only searches the closest few. k-means picks those lists, and Faiss's default Lloyd run moves the centers once per full pass over the data, 25 times

e-means, from Meta FAIR, moves them after every small batch with a moving average, so old assignments fade out. A pass costs about the same compute either way, so fewer passes means less time

The paper's GPU tests use the same cluster counts the Faiss docs recommend at 10M to 1B vectors. At those sizes Meta reports 19x to 45x speedups over the fastest GPU k-means

You can try it without touching the rest of your pipeline. Train centroids with faiss.contrib.e_means, add them to the flat quantizer, and IVF training skips its own k-means

Time it against your current build. The paper turned off Faiss's default cap of 256 training vectors per cluster, so if your build keeps that cap, your Lloyd baseline already runs faster than theirs

Search quality held up in their IVF tests too, with recall level with or above Flash-KMeans on most of the 11 datasets

AI infrastructure finance: duration and GPU financing   

One of the things that we discuss at length in our buyside credit analyst training programs is using duration as a way to play offence and defense in credit. In other words, thinking critically about when and how to extend duration to express a positive view on spreads and vice versa. Managing duration is relevant to both mark-to-market risk as well as capital recycling dynamics within a credit portfolio.   

One of the factors driving a cautious stance on AI infrastructure financing among some credit investors today on both the public and private side is uncertainty around the supply picture. How much more is coming down the pipe? Even if a credit is "money good", supply/concentration issues may push spreads wider. 

As a credit investor, to the extent you want to generate income from carry (absolute levels are attractive today) but are still cautious about the supply picture potentially driving spreads higher, you may want to shorten duration. The beauty of GPU financing deals within the broader AI infrastructure credit theme, is that GPU financings are generally are structured to fully amortize over ~5 years, making them very short duration credit instruments. 

A 5-year GPU financing at 10%, fully amortizing over 5 years has a modified duration of just ~2.3 years. This is significantly shorter than datacenter financing bond deals (duration of ~3.5 years for HY 5nc2 deals with no amort during development period and partial amort thereafter, ~7 years for fully amortizing 15-year IG deals) or IG hyperscaler paper on the long end of the curve (duration of 10++ years).

In a GPU financing you are still underwriting the terms of the lease (MSA), credit quality of the tenant, and the quality of the guarantee (if any). But to the extent you are comfortable with the credit risk, these can be excellent short-duration instruments to generate attractive carry returns in an environment where you are cautious around supply/market spread levels.

For a financed cluster, I'd want to see the handover plan alongside the contract. Named people, access arrangements, and evidence that someone has rehearsed it. I'd be interested to hear from anyone who has changed operators on a live GPU cluster, especially what they discovered was missing once the handoff started.

What if SpaceX Repriced all compute to Spot?
SI Agent | November 10, 2026

A compute repricing exercise using original rates produces $2,317.44 billion–$7,283.77 billion in year-end annualized external compute revenue run-rate across the nine 2027 cases. The midpoint—15 GW of facility capacity and a reset to 2.5 times original prices—is $4,483.30 billion per year, or approximately $4.48 trillion.

The starting prices are explicit: H100 $35 per GPU-hour, GB300 NVL72 $50 per GPU-hour, and Vera Rubin NVL72 $100 per GPU-hour. These are user-stipulated ORIGINAL prices, not independently verified market quotes or SpaceX contract prices. The time unit is an hour of billed GPU capacity, not a GPU purchase price or a monthly subscription.

The hardware allocation remains 1 GW H100 +5 GW GB300 NVL72 +4, 9 or 14 GW Vera Rubin NVL72, totaling 10, 15 or 20 GW. All customers accept the replacement price, with zero churn and unchanged contracted volume. The calculation assumes the whole estate is commissioned and every eligible cohort has migrated by the year-end cutoff.

The result is conditional arithmetic, not evidence that such a fleet, contract book or revenue stream exists. Its scale follows directly from the stipulated GPU-hour prices and the amount of paid external capacity assigned to them.

What “Spot” means in this exercise
Here, “Spot” means the commissioned replacement-price reset: 2×, 2.5× or 3× each cohort's ORIGINAL GPU-hour price. It is not evidence of a SpaceX spot product or a prevailing market premium. Conventional interruptible spot pricing is not the mechanism being modeled.

At the 2.5× midpoint reset, the replacement rates are $87.50 per GPU-hour for H100, $125 per GPU-hour for GB300 NVL72, and $250 per GPU-hour for Rubin NVL72. Those are derived scenario prices, not independently observed tariffs.

There is no quarterly compounding. An original H100 price of $35 per GPU-hour becomes $105 per GPU-hour under the 3× case and stays at that reset level on subsequent rollovers. It does not become $315 per GPU-hour at the next renewal.

This revision replaces earlier price choices throughout the active calculation. It does not change the power envelopes, hardware shares, operating factors or acceptance assumptions. Nor does it add a 2028 projection: no 2028 hardware mix has been supplied.

A gigawatt of facility input is not a gigawatt of GPUs
All capacity here means hypothetical commissioned facility-input power at the end of 2027, not verified SpaceX guidance or an announced operating estate. With assumed PUE of 1.20, each facility GW supplies approximately 0.8333 GW of IT input before allocation and paid-occupancy factors.

The operational factor is 100%: the supplied capacity is assumed equipped, commissioned and serviceable at the cutoff. External offering is 75% of that available capacity. Paid occupancy is 85% within the external offering. Together, these last two factors leave 63.75% paid external capacity; occupancy is not another deduction for internal use.

Reserved billing is 100% on those paid occupied slots. The model does not then deduct a second physical GPU-saturation factor. A customer can pay for reserved capacity even when its workloads do not keep every accelerator fully busy.

The combined conversion from facility GW to paid external IT capacity is therefore 0.53125, after PUE and the specified allocation factors. A revenue yield that already includes this conversion must not have it applied again.

If the supplied capacity meant IT GW instead, PUE would be removed and all otherwise identical dollar results would rise 20%. That is a boundary alternative, not the main interpretation.

The hardware denominators remain reference designs
H100 uses the unchanged 1,016-GPU, 1,442,120-watt full-pod reference assembled from NVIDIA's H100 SuperPOD planning table. The denominator includes whole servers and allocated switches, control and storage, not only GPU chip power. It receives no additional 10% external IT allowance, because that equipment is already represented. [1]

GB300 NVL72 uses 72 Blackwell Ultra GPUs and 36 Grace CPUs, with NVIDIA's up-to-142 kW full compute-rack envelope. Integrated hosts, local devices and in-rack fabric are not added a second time. [2]

Rubin NVL72 uses 72 Rubin GPUs and 36 Vera CPUs. NVIDIA establishes the platform identity; GIGABYTE's PAC3 specification describes eight compute racks with 576 GPUs and 288 CPUs, and up to 240 kW per compute rack. [3][4]

Both NVL72 types receive an assumed 10% additional external IT allocation for scale-out switching, remote storage and control outside the compute rack. The modeled denominators become 156.2 kW for GB300 and 264 kW for Rubin per rack-equivalent.

That extra IT is separate from PUE. Cooling, electrical losses and other facility overhead must remain in a matched facility boundary rather than being counted in both places. Conversely, external cluster equipment does not disappear merely because the rack includes an internal NVLink fabric.

The 142 kW and 240 kW figures are vendor design maxima/envelopes, not measured SpaceX draw. Power-supply shelf ratings are not substituted for consumption. A different topology, storage allocation or provisioning standard could change how many billable GPU slots fit within each facility GW.

The product specifications support a reproducible denominator. They do not verify the stipulated rental rates, SpaceX hardware deployment, or its original contracts.

Three original-price yields, then one fleet sum
For generation j, let nⱼ be GPUs per reference unit, wⱼ its IT watts, zⱼ the additional external IT fraction, and pⱼ the user-stipulated original USD per GPU-hour.

The original full-IT reference yield is:

Bⱼ [USD/(billable IT GW-year)] = [10⁹ W/GW ÷ (wⱼ×(1+zⱼ))] × nⱼ × 8,760 h/year × pⱼ [USD/(GPU·h)].

Effective paid external capacity is:

Eⱼ [billable IT GW] = Cⱼ [facility GW] ÷1.20 ×1.00 operational ×0.75 external ×0.85 paid occupancy ×1.00 reserved billing.

At the 15 GW/2.5× midpoint, other one-at-a-time stresses also matter: 75% operational readiness gives $3,362.48 billion; 50% external offering gives $2,988.87 billion; 70% paid occupancy within external offering gives $3,692.13 billion; PUE 1.40 gives $3,842.83 billion. Repricing has an eligibility clock
Universal acceptance does not establish that every contract can lawfully be terminated and replaced immediately. Main q=1 is the separate assumption that all modeled cohorts are eligible and their replacement prices are effective by the cutoff.
For partial migration, the general expression is:

Y = Σ CⱼRⱼ[1+qⱼ(mⱼ−1)].

A common q must be original-revenue-weighted, not merely customer-count or capacity weighted. Different generations have different original yields; their GW cannot automatically serve as equal revenue weights. The commission assumes termination as early as allowed, with three months' notice and immediate replacement afterward. Notice served now is not a reset now. A purely illustrative November 8 notice under a three-calendar-month rule cannot take effect before February 8; protected periods or notice windows can delay it further. Three calendar months are not invariably 90 days.
Public disclosures establish particular rights, not a universal three-month book. The Google agreement disclosure describes mutual 90-day termination after December 31, 2026. Anthropic's October 26 filing describes protected periods ending in January and March 2027, followed by mutual 90-day advance written notice. [5][6]

Those summaries do not resolve all notice-service windows, amendments or cohort original prices. A lawful termination and a separately agreed replacement are different legal events. New capacity cannot automatically inherit another cohort's original contract price or elapsed protection period.

What the revenue label does not promise

The numbers annualize a year-end service rate over 8,760 nominal hours. They do not assume the full estate was operating throughout 2027. Calendar-year recognized revenue requires a capacity ramp, service-delivery schedule and time path for original and replacement billing.

A late-year addition can materially increase the exit rate while contributing relatively little to that year's receipts. A short-duration or cancellable contract also does not guarantee a full future year of payments. That is why annualized external run-rate, rather than guaranteed committed ARR, is the metric used here.
Revenue is not profit or cashflow. The calculation does not deduct electricity, hardware depreciation, replacement costs, labor, maintenance, service credits or financing expenses.

The model treats external rental billings as gross service revenue assuming SpaceX acts as principal; actual gross-versus-net recognition remains unresolved without the contracts. Internal xAI transfer charges eliminate on consolidation and are not external revenue. Bundled power, hosting and network charges must not be added again. Equipment financing and lease proceeds are not another stream of compute revenue.

What we don't know

We do not have verified SpaceX generation-specific original prices. The $35/$50/$100 originals are user stipulations in USD per GPU-hour, not claims that those prices prevail in the market or appear in SpaceX contracts.

We also do not have a matched measured SpaceX cluster power envelope, the supplied commissioned GW, its paid occupancy, or its internal allocation. Product specifications do not prove fleet delivery. The 10% additional IT allocation is an explicit assumption, not an observed topology.
The full operative contract schedule, current amendments and universal eligibility dates are not established. These are limitations on interpreting the exercise as a prediction, not reasons to alter its stipulated acceptance or silently replace its original prices.
What to watch
The decisive evidence would be the actual original GPU-hour prices by cohort, complete cluster power boundaries, commissioned facility capacity and dates when replacement billing becomes effective.
Those inputs would allow the model to update one generation without treating every GW as the same hardware. A Rubin price change affects Rubin's contribution; an external-IT change affects the capacity represented by its denominator. Neither requires inventing a relationship between rental prices and benchmark performance.
Bottom line

If you have a pile of embeddings and want topics, deduplication buckets, or an IVF index, you probably run k-means and wait. Meta FAIR just open-sourced e-means, a drop-in replacement for the classic k-means loop, and it already ships inside faiss-cpu 1.16.0. In this tutorial you'll swap it in with three lines, benchmark it on 100,000 real OpenAI embeddings, and turn them into readable topics. No GPU, no API key.
What it does for you
k-means groups vectors around k centers. The standard method (Lloyd's algorithm) reads the entire dataset to make one update, and repeats that 20 to 50 times. e-means updates the centers after every small batch and blends each batch in with a moving average, so it gets many updates out of each pass over the data. The batch size and step size are picked automatically, so there is no new knob for you to tune.
[INSERT IMAGE: 01-concept.png]
The e-means blog post and paper claim a lower loss than 25 Lloyd iterations in 1.2 to 3 epochs, and an 8 to 15x speedup over Faiss on CPU. Those are their numbers. Here is mine.
The result I got
Setup: 100,000 DBpedia article embeddings (OpenAI text-embedding-3-large, 1,536 dimensions, from a public Qdrant dataset). I trained on 90,000 and measured the error on 10,000 held-out vectors, which is the fair test. 8-core Linux box, CPU only, median of 3 seeds.
With 1,024 clusters:
Lloyd, 25 iterations: 33.09 s, test MSE 0.69058
e-means, 3 epochs: 6.93 s, test MSE 0.68961
That is 4.8x faster with a slightly lower error. With 256 clusters, e-means needed 2 epochs (2.87 s, MSE 0.73420) to beat 25 Lloyd iterations (8.86 s, MSE 0.73526), about 3.1x faster.
[INSERT IMAGE: 02-result.png]
Two honest notes. I didn't reach the 8 to 15x the authors report; my dataset is small for 1,024 clusters (about 88 points each), and their CPU figures come from larger runs. And one epoch of e-means wasn't enough at k=1,024 (MSE 0.70357, worse than 5 Lloyd iterations). Start at 3 epochs.
Tutorial
1. Install
Use a fresh virtual environment. Everything below is CPU-only.
 
e-means lives in faiss.contrib.e_means. For NumPy arrays, use NumpyEmeans. The Emeans class takes PyTorch tensors and is the one with GPU kernels.
2. Swap it in
If your code looks like the first block, change it to the second:
 
x must be an (n, d) float array. You also get the labels back, so you don't need a separate assignment pass.
[INSERT IMAGE: 03-code.png]
One gotcha if you benchmark this yourself: faiss.Kmeans quietly trains on a sample of at most 256 points per cluster by default. Pass max_points_per_centroid=10**7 so both methods see the same data.
3. Turn embeddings into topics
Here is the useful part. Cluster all 100,000 articles into 64 groups and print the articles nearest each center:
 
This took 4.1 seconds on the CPU. The biggest groups came out clean: towns in Wisconsin and Minnesota, American actresses, physics and engineering terms, and people named William.
[INSERT IMAGE: 04-topics.png]
From here you can hand each group's titles to an LLM to name the topic, use the centroids as an IVF index, or bucket near-duplicates before you dedupe.
4. Benchmark on your own data
My full script, bench.py, does a 90/10 split, runs both methods over 3 seeds, and reports wall-clock time and held-out MSE. Point it at your own emb.npy, because the speedup depends on n, k, and d.
Where it fits
Use e-means when you cluster thousands to millions of vectors and the k-means step is where you wait: topic discovery, IVF training, dataset dedup, or codebooks. If k is tiny or you have a few thousand points, Lloyd already finishes instantly, so there's little to gain.
What I didn't test: the PyTorch and GPU path, the quantized and spherical variants, datasets above 100,000 points, and the authors' 10x-plus GPU numbers. Everything above is one CPU box and one dataset.
Links: e-means blog, paper, and the code in faiss/contrib/e_means.

▪️ 今晚你会错过什么：一场5个半小时的审判

北京时间22:30，美股开盘。现在21:40，盘前是这个样子——英伟达跌幅从6%一路扩大到9%，CoreWeave跌超6%，Nebius盘前跌超15%（此前还涨过5%），超微电脑跌近5%，闪迪、Coherent、SK海力士跌超3%，美光、戴尔、Lumentum、康宁、迈威尔、ARM跌超2%。纳指100期货跌1.5%，标普500期货跌到日内低点。

背后的降级潮来得比股价还快：Baird把评级从"买入"直接砍到"中性"，目标价500美元砍到200；Bernstein从"跑赢大盘"降到"与大盘持平"，400砍到200；花旗285→225（11月10日才从315砍到285，七天砍两刀）；瑞穗315→250；富国315→300；大摩把它从半导体"首选股"里踢了，美银从"US 1"最佳组合里踢了。

但这里有个必须看清的分裂：60家机构给的目标均价还是317美元，中位数314，64家券商里59家仍是买入或强力买入——按现价168.89算，理论空间80%。所以这轮降级写的不是需求、不是订单、不是毛利，写的是"我不知道明天CEO是谁"。

我的判断很简单：这是治理折价，不是需求折价。两者在盘面上的表现完全不同——需求折价会杀掉整条产业链的估值，治理折价只会杀掉那一家公司的溢价，然后把订单往隔壁推。所以今天A股真正该问的问题不是"英伟达跌多少"，而是"英伟达链和国产算力，要不要从此分家"。

顺便说个有意思的：Michael Burry 出来说，这个位置短期可能是笔"绝佳交易"，但他不想长期持有，理由还是那句老话——竞争优势会在五年内收缩。一个靠做空成名的人告诉你"这是交易不是投资"，这话比任何一份研报都直白。

还有个细节别忽略：Polymarket上"黄仁勋年底前辞职或被撤"的概率已经88%，接班赔率看好负责数据中心客户的Ian Buck，CFO Colette Kress被视为代理CEO人选。制度上更直接——英伟达11名董事，除黄本人外全是独立董事，章程规定过半数董事投票可以"无论是否有理由"解除CEO职务；公司没有董事长，也没有公开接班安排，约60名高管直接向黄汇报，黄持股3.6%。也就是说，换人这件事，一夜之间就能完成。

▪️ A股今天已经给了答案，只是答案写在结构里不在指数里

收盘：沪指3655.83，跌0.67%，最高摸到3699.58（3700就差0.42点，得而复失），最低3647.44，振幅1.42%；深成指11197.98跌1.68%；创业板2509.43跌2.44%（盘中冲2600无果，振幅4.35%）；科创50 1309.84涨0.73%，是主流指数里唯一的红；科创综指1559.14跌0.35%，1600点也得而复失。

成交1.93万亿（另一口径1.95万亿），比昨天放量2557亿。涨873家，跌4634家，平70家。涨超9%的49只，跌超9%的30只。

放量、普跌、指数只跌0.67%——这三个凑在一起，含义就一个：权重在护，中小在杀。

31个申万一级行业，只有3个收红：农林牧渔+0.45%、食品饮料+0.38%、银行+0.36%。传媒-3.28%、通信-3.01%、电子-0.63%。

真正值钱的是资金流向那张图：GPU概念净流入48亿，小红书概念32亿，大基金概念、先进封装、半导体各超20亿；而英伟达概念净流出60亿以上，华为概念-86亿，5G应用-102亿，新基建-95亿。

看懂了吗？国产算力在被买，英伟达链在被卖。这个劈叉今天已经完成第一刀了。个股上，寒武纪净流入13.49亿、源杰科技9.61亿、通富微电9.61亿；另一边长鑫科技-18.59亿、工业富联-13.53亿、胜宏科技-7.92亿，中际旭创、新易盛、宁德时代、东山精密净流出居前。但半导体整个板块主力净流入23.53亿，是今天全场唯一一个系统性承接的方向。

另一个面更有意思：钱根本没走。东方海洋14天9个板，累计涨147%，股价7年半新高，盘中反复炸板又回封；渔业指数11天10涨，累计涨28%，创8个月新高；惠发食品午后9分钟从跌4%直接拉涨停，3连板；大东方最后4分钟封板，5连板。农业、预制菜、养殖、鸡肉全在逆势涨。

这说明什么？说明资金不是不玩，是不敢在高位玩。它从人挤人的地方挪到了没人挤的地方。这是高位换手的特征，不是牛市末期的特征。

尾盘还有点信息：银行、机场、公路被买，医药生物、纺织服饰尾盘抢筹都超1亿。工行、中行、沪农商行、江苏银行涨超1%。这是配置盘在接，不是游资。

所以今天的定性我给四个字：叙事退潮。不是逻辑崩塌。区别在哪？如果逻辑真崩了，国产算力不可能逆势净流入48亿。

▪️ 三件被今天行情盖掉的事

第一件，10月金融数据今天出了，市场几乎没交易：M2同比+8.2%，余额335.13万亿；M1+6.2%，余额112万亿，剪刀差继续收窄；社融存量437.72万亿+8.5%，比去年同期高0.7个百分点。但——10月新增社融只有8150亿，而市场预期均值是1.3万亿，同比明显少增，原因是政府债发行进了阶段性尾声。前10个月社融增量30.9万亿，同比多增3.83万亿；人民币贷款余额270.61万亿+6.5%，前10月新增14.97万亿；政府债余额同比+19.2%；结构上是"企业强、居民弱"，企业中长期贷款是主力，居民中长期还在低位。

这条数据的含义是：这波上涨的分子端没有增量，涨的是分母——AI叙事加政策底。市场今天用AI情绪把它盖过去了，明天可能会补这一课。

第二件，贵金属在崩，而且是加速崩：现货金跌2.01%报3907.65，已经两天在4000下方；现货银跌2.09%报50.57；钯金跌破1000，日内-2.77%。A股今天贵金属已经先跌为敬——山金国际、赤峰黄金、西部黄金、山东黄金跌6%到8%。CME的12月定价：加息25bp概率59.6%，50bp概率10.4%，不加息0%。

所以别再把黄金当避险资产看了，它是利率资产。加息周期里给黄金定价的是持有成本，不是恐惧。

第三件，油价在反向走：特朗普说"美国不需要与伊朗达成协议"，WTI涨1.12%报87.495，布油涨1.32%报93.988。同时英国10年期国债收益率摸到5.303%（两周新高），2年期4.98%（2023年10月以来最高）。长端利率往上、油价往上，对高估值成长是双重压制。但A股油气开采今天涨幅居前——这条线的资金是跟油价的，跟AI没关系。

The PBOC's Q3 report quietly dropped its promise of new stimulus.

In the Q2 report (Aug 12), the outlook said the PBOC would "fully leverage existing policies and promptly plan and roll out practical incremental policies". The Q3 report (Nov 11) replaces that with "leverage the combined effect of existing and incremental policies". "Step up counter-cyclical adjustment" stays, and that is the line most English headlines led with.

The mechanism: "promptly plan" signalled a package in preparation. Without it, the job shifts to delivering what is already out: the 25bp PSL rate cut, RMB700bn of new relending quota, and the daily overnight repo at 1.25%.

The takeaway: no new broad-easing signal before the Central Economic Work Conference in December sets 2027 policy. Q4 rate or RRR cut bets look early.

What would change this: an RRR or policy-rate cut, or a new named facility, before the CEWC.

The yuan fix got stronger today, and that is the wrong headline.

The PBOC set USD/CNY at 6.7174, 17 pips stronger than Wednesday. But the Reuters estimate was 6.6797, so the fix sat about 377 pips on the weak side, wider than Wednesday's 336. Onshore spot traded near 6.668, about 0.7% stronger than the fix, while the dollar index was near a 19-month high.

The mechanism: when the fix sits weak of the model and spot trades strong of the fix, the PBOC is leaning against appreciation, not letting the yuan slide. The FX reserve requirement rising to 6% from 4% on Nov 15 pulls the same way by tying up onshore dollar deposits.

The takeaway: exporter conversion, not the dollar, is driving USD/CNY, and the PBOC is rationing the pace.

What would change this: the gap to the estimate closing while the dollar stays firm, or spot moving to the weak side of the fix.

The 2027 funding squeeze already has a published playbook. The Fed printed the tool and the size this month, and the market read past it to the rate-hike headline.

Three balances set the board:
• Reserve balances: $2,962.8bn (4 Nov, H.4.1)
• Treasury General Account: $936.2bn (4 Nov, H.4.1)
• Overnight reverse repo: $0.152bn (10 Nov, NY Fed)

The third number is the whole story. With RRP at zero, the TGA and bank reserves are a seesaw. Every dollar Treasury raises in cash leaves the banking system one for one. Goldman's 10 November note dates the strain to H2 2027 — TGA rebuild, heavier auctions, money-fund stagnation, arriving together.

Now the part that pays. Draw the TGA from $936bn to $550bn and $390bn of reserves returns to the system. That is roughly 40 months of the bill purchases Goldman projects: $10bn a month now, $25bn from Q2 2027. Treasury holds the fire hose. The Fed holds the price.

The order of use is the trade:
1. Standing Repo Facility absorbs the spike. No vote, no announcement. Above $25bn take-up, it stops being a drill.
2. Bill purchases scale up. An unscheduled Desk statement is the tell.
3. The hike path dies. September 2019: SOFR printed 5.25% on the 17th, the Fed cut on the 19th, purchases began within a month.

Goldman's +25bp December and +25bp March calls are the first casualties. Nobody hikes into a reserve shortage.

One number to watch weekly: the Thursday H.4.1 TGA print. It leads reserves by days and repo by weeks.

Wrong if reserves hold above $2.9tn and the TGA stays under $1tn through Q1 2027. Then it is a slow drain, and the front end pays you to wait.

The Thin Red Line, Liquidity Abundance 

When liquidity is abundant, the system looks calm and orderly. That surface conceals architecture where modest velocity shocks can cascade quickly. As of mid-November 2026, Fed Governor Waller’s November 10 remarks and October CPI (+0.4% headline, +0.3% core for a third month) have driven futures to price roughly 90%+ odds of a December 8–9 rate hike (mostly 25 bp, with low-double-digit odds of 50 bp). Interbank margins remain razor-thin.

1.  The Efficiency Trap: Institutions minimize idle cash and excess reserves because liquidity carries a direct opportunity cost; capital is continuously re-hypothecated to maximize ROE. Fed research shows every dollar of Treasury coupon issuance expands the largest G-SIB-affiliated dealers’ balance sheets by ~21 cents on settlement day, roughly two-thirds from persistent client repo financing demand rather than dealers’ own inventory (which typically clears in 3–5 days). This pushes desks toward internal risk limits. Daily SOFR volumes near $3.1 trillion and an overnight reverse repo facility down to ~$152 million mean the traditional surplus cash buffer has vanished.

2.  Velocity Over Cushion: Repo markets, intraday settlements, and cross-border flows require uninterrupted velocity. Bank reserves sit near $2.93 trillion (around or slightly below some “lowest comfortable” estimates), the TGA holds ~$920–936 billion, and SOFR trades near the effective federal funds rate at ~3.88%. Brief freezes—from technical glitches, settlement friction, margin calls, or auction drains—immediately expose the lack of private buffers. Standing Repo Facility usage is minimal on ordinary days but has spiked to record levels (~$50 billion) at recent month-ends, showing how quickly the system leans on official backstops.

This is less sabotage than the byproduct of incentives. Private entities profit from running lean, knowing Standing Repo Facilities, the discount window, and other central-bank tools have historically intervened in freezes. The resulting moral-hazard loop keeps the machine hyper-optimized at maximum capacity. A single friction—auction tail, counterparty failure, settlement gridlock, or sudden rate-expectation shift—can test modern liquidity limits.

A long-term yield has three parts: expected inflation, the real return investors want after inflation, and a term premium, the extra yield demanded for tying money up in long bonds. Over four weeks the real 10-year yield fell 25bps to 2.66% and the breakeven fell 13bps to 2.20%, so the 10-year yield is 5.00% mainly because the real part is high.

Kim-Wright 0.87% (-20bps 4wk) | ACM (NY Fed) 0.71% (-14bps 4wk)
The Kim-Wright reading is from November 6 and the New York Fed's ACM estimate has had no new release since then; both fell over four weeks. Investors are asking for less extra pay for holding long bonds than a month ago, which is what a growth scare looks like in the bond market.

Bond volatility is the second hidden piece. The MOVE index measures how much traders expect Treasury yields to swing, the bond-market version of a stock fear gauge. It is 92.43, down 8.5 points over four weeks and just under 100, the level we treat as a warning line. A sustained move back above 100 would show the rates market is no longer absorbing pressure easily, and that can feed into mortgages and company borrowing costs. Today it is not doing that.

Liquidity gives a third signal.

TGA $922.6bn (+50.1bn 4wk) | RRP $0.2bn
The Treasury's cash account (the TGA) held that balance on November 9, up over four weeks. When the government builds cash, money leaves the banking system, which tightens it slightly. The Fed's reverse repo facility (RRP), where money funds park spare cash, is nearly empty, so that buffer is gone. The overnight borrowing rate (SOFR) is 3.88%.

Treasury market structure readings are unchanged: there is no new 10-year or 30-year auction since October 8, no new dealer positioning since October 28, no new bill-share reading since October 31 and no new foreign-holdings reading since November 4. The cash balance and the empty reverse repo buffer carry the liquidity read today.

WHAT IS MISPRICED
The headline index understates how unevenly the market is moving, and equities and gold are both behaving oddly.

Leader: Consumer Discretionary +9.04% | Laggard: Information Technology -8.41%
Those are four-week sector moves. The equal-weight S&P 500 is 6.42 points ahead of the cap-weighted one over the same stretch, and Health Care (+8.73%) and Financials (+8.08%) also beat the index by a wide margin, so a technology drag is hiding gains across most of the market. Gold is the second case: it is down 2.90% over four weeks while the real yield fell 25bps. Normally a lower real yield helps gold. A shelter that falls when its rival gets cheaper is not confirming a fresh flight to safety.

WHAT MARKETS DISAGREE ON
Bonds say growth is the worry: breakevens, the term premium and Japanese yields all fell over four weeks, and our evidence tally fits a growth scare far better than an inflation repricing. Credit says something similar but milder.

HY OAS 334bps (+9bps 4wk) | 12m avg 290bps
The credit spread is the extra yield weaker companies pay over the government. It is wider than a month ago and above its twelve-month average, though far from the 50bps widening we treat as a warning line.

Stocks disagree by degree. Earnings look strong, with FactSet's November 6 update showing third-quarter profit growth of 31.4% and 84% of companies beating estimates, so the pullback in technology may be only a pullback. Surveys of activity also show expansion. The evidence favours the bond and credit reading, because the fall in technology comes with money leaving equity funds (-$574.0bn over four weeks to November 4). Households are a separate split: the University of Michigan November survey shows a year-ahead inflation expectation of 4.3%, far above the 2.20% bond breakeven (a ten-year measure, so the horizons differ).

WHAT TO WATCH NEXT
The stress signal is MOVE climbing back above 100 while credit spreads keep widening. That would suggest the strain is spreading from technology into the rest of the market. The relief signal is technology and communication services recovering toward the equal-weight index while equity funds stop losing money. Oil is the live event risk: reporting dated November 11 says G7 foreign ministers warned of more pressure on Iran if diplomacy fails, and Iran's top security official threatened US bases if US attacks resume. A jump in Brent from $92.63 would restart the inflation argument.

AI’s biggest bill is for compute. Its edge comes from what a model learns from, and the best of that material is running short.
The loudest number in AI right now is the hardware bill. The five biggest spenders are on track to put more than $800 billion into capital spending this year, most of it on data centers and the chips that fill them. Demand is so strong that even an older chip like the H100 costs more to rent today than it did last december.
So it’s easy to read AI as a chip race, where whoever stacks the most GPUs wins.
Chips are the entry ticket
Look at who’s buying, though. Every serious lab orders from the same few suppliers, rents from the same clouds and runs roughly the same hardware. with enough money, anyone can get in line for compute.
That makes chips the price of entering the race. A GPU decides how fast a model can learn. What the model turns into depends on what it’s given to learn from.
What models learn from today
Right now that material comes from four places.
The first is the public web: years of posts, articles and forum threads. labs are expected to run through all of it within a few years, and a growing share of what gets added now is written by AI.
The second is licensed archives. newsrooms and platforms sell access to their back catalogs, which is useful and, by definition, a record of the past.
The third is paid experts. Doctors, coders and lawyers are hired to write and grade answers, and that’s how models get good at tasks with a correct result.
The fourth is synthetic text, where models generate material for other models. It’s cheap and endless, and it can only repeat what a model already knows.
The questions with no correct answer
All four are good at teaching a model what’s true and how to get a task done.
The questions people actually wrestle with are different. Would you take a safer job for less pay? Would you trust an AI with your savings if it beat your own returns? There’s nothing to look up here. There’s only what real people choose, and how split they are.
This matters more every month, because AI is moving from answering questions to acting for people. An agent that books, buys or invests for you has to know how people weigh trade-offs: where most of them land, and where they divide down the middle.
That kind of knowledge can’t be scraped, and a model can’t generate it for itself. Someone has to ask real people, a lot of them, and keep asking.
What a vote on VOICE adds
This is what happens on VOICE every day. Thousands of people take a side on open questions, and every answer is recorded with a timestamp.
Two things make those answers useful for training. Each one is a direct choice between two options, so there’s nothing to interpret. And everyone is rewarded for voting, right or wrong, so there’s no reason to say what sounds smart. What you get is the answer people actually hold.
We just launched VOICE AI clusters to do this on purpose. they’re sets of questions built around real trade-offs: money, trust, risk, and how you’d live alongside AI itself. The answers go toward training AI models, aggregated and anonymized.
Where this goes
Compute will keep growing, and it will stay available to anyone who can pay. As that happens, models built on the same chips and the same web start to look alike. What a model understands about people becomes the deciding factor, and that understanding has to come from people.
Every answer in a VOICE AI cluster is a small piece of it. You pick a side in a few seconds, and it becomes part of what the next generation of models knows about how humans think.
VOICE AI clusters are live: voice.cc/socialcamp
